title: Adapter Pattern
summary: Wrapping one interface so it satisfies another, without touching either side — the pattern behind every third-party SDK wrapper and legacy migration shim.

slides.markdown:
An **Adapter** converts the interface one class exposes into the interface a client expects, so two pieces of code that were never designed to talk can work together — without modifying either one.

Think of a physical plug adapter: it doesn't rewire the wall socket or the laptop charger, it just sits between them so the shapes match. In software this shows up constantly — wrapping a third-party library, bridging an old API into a new one, or gluing together two systems built years apart.

slides.sectionTitle: The problem: two incompatible interfaces that need to work together
slides.markdown:
Say you built your app against a `Logger` interface with a `log(message: string)` method. Now you need to integrate a well-tested third-party analytics library that only exposes `writeEntry(level: int, text: string, timestamp: long)`. The library is solid — rewriting it isn't an option — but its interface doesn't match what the rest of your code calls.

You have three bad options: rewrite the library (risky, wasteful), rewrite your codebase to call `writeEntry` everywhere (invasive, spreads a dependency), or scatter conditional glue code at every call site (unmaintainable). None of these isolate the mismatch to one place.

slides.sectionTitle: Adapter: wrap one interface to satisfy another, without changing either
slides.markdown:
The fix: write one small class that implements the interface your code expects (`Logger`) and internally delegates to the interface you actually have (the analytics library). Your `AnalyticsLoggerAdapter.log(message)` translates the call into `writeEntry(INFO, message, now())` and forwards it.

Neither the `Logger` interface nor the analytics library changes at all — the adapter is the only place that knows both shapes exist. Callers keep writing `logger.log(...)` exactly as before; swapping the adapter later (a different analytics vendor) touches one file, not the whole app.

The client only ever sees the interface it expects. The adapter is the sole class aware that a translation is happening — the adaptee never even knows it's being adapted.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: object adapter (composition) vs class adapter (inheritance)
slides.markdown:
Two ways to build the same adapter, with different trade-offs.

| | Object adapter | Class adapter |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Holds an instance of the adaptee, delegates calls | Inherits from the adaptee, overrides/adds methods |
| Language needs | Works anywhere — just composition | Needs multiple inheritance (C++) or similar |
| Flexibility | Can adapt any subclass of the adaptee at runtime | Locked to one adaptee class at compile time |
| Common in | Java, C#, TypeScript, Python | C++, occasionally Python mixins |

**How to decide:** default to the object adapter — composition over inheritance, and it works in every mainstream language without fighting the type system.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: adapting a legacy XmlLogger to a new Logger interface
Pitfall: an adapter that leaks the adaptee's exceptions/semantics untranslated
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "The adapter just forwards the call, so I don't need to touch error handling."

**Why it's wrong:** if `write_xml_entry` throws a library-specific `XmlSerializationError` and the adapter lets it propagate unchanged, every caller of `Logger.log()` now has to know about an exception type that has nothing to do with logging — the interface boundary just leaked straight through it.

**Correct model:** the adapter owns translating failures, not just method signatures. Catch the adaptee's exceptions and re-raise (or swallow, per the `Logger` contract) something the interface actually promises — silence isn't a fix, cross-boundary leakage is the bug.

slides.sectionTitle: Where Adapter shows up: third-party SDK wrappers, legacy migration seams
slides.markdown:
You'll meet Adapter constantly: wrapping a payment gateway's SDK behind your own `PaymentProcessor` interface so switching from Stripe to Adyen doesn't touch business logic; bridging a legacy on-prem API into a new microservices contract during a migration; or adapting a cloud provider's SDK (AWS S3 vs GCS) behind one `BlobStore` interface so the rest of the app stays cloud-agnostic.

**When NOT to use it:** if you control both interfaces and they're diverging for no good reason, fix the interface instead of adapting around the mismatch forever — an adapter is for boundaries you don't own, not a permanent patch over your own design debt.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: Adapter vs Facade — translating one interface vs simplifying many
slides.markdown:
Both patterns wrap something, but for opposite reasons.

| | Adapter | Facade |
|---|---|---|
| Goal | Make an existing interface match one the client expects | Provide a new, simpler interface over a complex subsystem |
| Interfaces involved | Exactly one incompatible interface | Many subsystem classes, no single expected shape |
| Adds new behavior? | No — pure translation | Sometimes coordinates, but shouldn't add business logic |
| Motivation | Compatibility | Simplicity |

**How to decide:** if you're translating a shape you didn't choose, it's Adapter; if you're hiding complexity you did choose, see [Facade](facade-pattern).
